title: Validator‑Guided Repair on a Shared Initial LLM Candidate: A Preregistered Paired Evaluation for Network Configuration Safety
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory experiment (PREREG‑CAND‑001‑VER‑GVR‑2026‑09‑01) to measure whether a deterministic network‑configuration validator plus a single allowed automated repair changes the executability status of the exact same sampled LLM candidate per intent (shared_initial_candidate semantics). Using the declared generator gpt‑5‑mini (hosted adapter label openai_responses) and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 on N = 200 paired intents (completed_episode_count = 400; model_calls_used = 200), every shared initial candidate passed validator checks so no repairs were attempted or applied (repair_attempt_count = 0; repair_applied_count = 0). Observed outcomes: baseline_success = 200/200, guarded_success = 200/200; paired contingency n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (bootstrap_seed = 1729; 10,000 resamples) = [0.0, 0.0]. We present artifact‑grounded methodology, detailed execution accounting, representative validator diagnostics that explain why repairs were not invoked, and a focused discussion clarifying the causal limits of the executed estimand and preregistered follow‑on designs required to measure repair efficacy under independent sampling, increased difficulty, or adversarial inputs.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) are being proposed to translate operator intent into device configuration sequences in network operations (NetOps). Applied naively, generated sequences can contain syntactic errors, incorrect sequencing, or fabricated fields that—if executed—could cause service disruption, policy violations, or security exposures. A common mitigation architecture is a generate→validate→repair (GVR) pipeline: generate candidate configuration(s), apply a deterministic validator to detect violations against intent and topology constraints, and trigger an automated repair when faults are detected. Prior work documents verifier‑guided improvements in adjacent domains (infrastructure‑as‑code, program repair) and advocates grounding and retrieval to reduce hallucination in operational text tasks; however, those demonstrations typically measure textual or code correctness rather than whether generated device commands would produce unsafe executable states when enacted on network elements.

This paper reports a fully preregistered, paired confirmatory experiment that implements a narrowly defined estimand: shared_initial_candidate semantics. For each intent we produced exactly one sampled initial generation and deterministically reused that same candidate for both the baseline (no validator/repair) and guarded (validator plus ≤1 automated repair permitted) episodes. Under these semantics any paired outcome difference can only arise from deterministic validation and any subsequent permitted repair acting on the identical candidate. The paper's contributions are (1) an artifact‑grounded report of the executed paired experiment with full execution accounting, (2) complete numeric inferential results and representative validator diagnostics showing why repairs were not invoked, and (3) a preregistered roadmap of concrete, artifact‑supported follow‑on estimand variants and experimental changes required to evaluate repair efficacy under independent sampling or adversarial conditions.
sections.related_work:
Three strands of verified literature motivated the design. First, surveys and empirical reports document hallucination and reliability issues for LLMs in operational contexts and motivate grounding and verification strategies [1]. Second, generate→validate→repair architectures (verifier‑guided feedback or policy‑guided repair) have demonstrated empirical correctness improvements in infrastructure‑as‑code and program repair tasks; these works motivated applying verifier guidance to NetOps configuration generation but do not evaluate execution‑level safety on network device state [2][3]. Third, NetOps‑specific capability evaluations emphasize intent translation and model competence but typically stop short of measuring whether generated commands are executable and safe in packet‑level simulation or device emulation [4].

Two methodologic gaps in the verified corpus informed experiment selection. There is limited evidence measuring whether verifier‑guided repair pipelines prevent unsafe executable states in network simulators; second, many prior demonstrations do not specify causal estimands that separate sampling variability from downstream validator/repair effects. Our paired shared_initial_candidate design intentionally isolates the latter causal mechanism so the experiment yields an unambiguous statement about validator/repair acting on identical generator outputs.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand. We preregistered all design choices before model calls (PREREG‑CAND‑001‑VER‑GVR‑2026‑09‑01). The primary estimand is the paired difference in the proportion of validator‑valid executable configurations between guarded and baseline conditions under shared_initial_candidate semantics. The confirmatory hypothesis (H1) posited that permitting the deterministic validator plus at most one automated repair (guarded) would reduce executable unsafe configurations relative to leaving the same initial candidate unguarded (baseline).

Design parameters. The sampling plan fixed task_count = 200 paired intents (planned_episode_count = 400). Generation semantics were explicitly shared_initial_candidate: exactly one initial generation per pair was sampled and reused by both conditions. The model provider label was openai_responses with declared_model_version = "gpt‑5‑mini"; model_calls_used = 200 (one shared initial generation per pair). The archived model_configuration.json records temperature = null/unset; we note explicitly that null/unset is not evidence of deterministic sampling and does not imply temperature = 0. The preregistration limited repairs to a maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1 in the guarded arm.

Task bank, contamination, and task selection. A deterministic task generator produced a fixed manifest of synthetic "intent_configuration_repair_v1" tasks with explicit initial_state, required_sequence, and difficulty annotations (for example, "safe_access_service_transfer", "rolling_access_vlan_migration"). Prior to model calls we executed the preregistered contamination checks (SHA‑256 exact‑match and n‑gram similarity) against repair and corpus artifacts; no exact‑match exclusions were flagged and the confirmatory sample executed intact. The task generator recorded generation_seed values to enable deterministic replay.

Validator, scoring, and outcome mapping. Scoring used deterministic_netops_validator_v5 with scoring_rule = "full_intent_constraint_validation." The validator parses the candidate command sequence, checks required_sequence and workflow_policies, and emits a structured trace containing validation_before and validation_after subtables, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, normalized_configuration, violation_codes, violation_count, and a repair_applied boolean. We mapped validator.valid = true to a binary "executable/valid" outcome for analysis. Under shared_initial_candidate semantics only a guarded repair (if triggered) could mutate the identical shared_initial_candidate; the baseline arm reused the same candidate unchanged.

Statistical analysis plan. The preregistered primary test was the exact two‑sided McNemar test on the 2×2 paired contingency table; paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI was computed with bootstrap_seed = 1729 and bootstrap_resamples = 10,000. Primary missingness policy: complete_pair_primary (exclude incomplete pairs). Planned sensitivity analysis: treat missing or failed episodes as unsafe (failure‑as‑zero). Exploratory subgroup analyses by declared difficulty pattern were predesignated exploratory and would be corrected by Benjamini–Hochberg FDR if performed.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and deterministic reconciliation. Execution completed without infrastructure failure. The execution manifest reports planned_episode_count = 400, completed_episode_count = 400, failed_episode_count = 0, and model_calls_used = 200. Analysis missingness_summary reports complete_pairs = 200 and zero failed or unscorable episodes. Deterministic reconciliation confirms that stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 200}, provider_call_audit.hosted_model_call_event_count = 200, cache_miss_count = 200, and cross_condition_cache_key_reuse_observed = false; all deterministic consistency checks passed.

Primary outcomes and inferential statistics. Analysis/condition_summary.csv records baseline_successes = 200/200 and guarded_successes = 200/200 (success_rate = 1.0 each). The paired contingency table observed n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI for the paired difference (bootstrap_seed = 1729; 10,000 resamples) = [0.0, 0.0]. These artifact‑recorded numbers appear verbatim in analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv and analysis/condition_summary.csv.

Repair activity and validator diagnostics. Across the confirmatory sample repair_attempt_count = 0 and repair_applied_count = 0: the validator did not flag any violations on any shared initial candidate, so the guarded repair path had no opportunity to execute. Representative per‑episode JSON artifacts (for example, execution/scoring/task‑000004‑baseline.json and task‑000004‑guarded.json) show identical shared_initial_candidate text and identical validation_after.normalized_configuration values. Representative shared_initial_candidate excerpt (task‑000004):

interface edge2 admin down
interface edge2 vlan 40
interface edge2 admin up
interface edge1 admin down

For that example parsed_command_count = 4, required_command_count = 4, and validator.valid = true. Similar diagnostics for task‑000005 and task‑000006 show parsed_command_count matching required_command_count and validator.valid = true. The absence of any violation_codes and violation_count = 0 in validation_after subtables explains the degenerate contingency: with no validator detections there was nothing for the repair step to act upon.

Contamination and provider audit summaries. Preexecution contamination checks produced an empty contamination_summary (no exact‑match flags). Provider audit traces record hosted_model_call_event_count = 200, completed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 200, and cache_miss_count = 200. No retrials or infrastructure restarts were recorded. The execution manifest includes preregistration_sha256 and artifact_hash_count = 1406, enabling independent verification of the run's integrity.

Compact repair summary requested by reviewers. Total_pairs = 200; repair_attempt_count = 0; repair_applied_count = 0. These counts derive directly from per‑episode validator_trace fields and are reflected in analysis artifacts archived in the bundle.
sections.discussion:
Estimand scope and causal interpretation. By design, shared_initial_candidate semantics remove sampling variability between conditions: each baseline/guarded pair begins from the identical sampled candidate. This design isolates the causal effect of deterministic validation and any permitted repair acting on that candidate. The executed estimand therefore answers whether deterministic validation plus a single permitted repair can change outcomes when faced with the exact same generator output. It does not evaluate whether guarded pipelines reduce generator error rates under independent per‑condition sampling, nor whether alternative generation strategies (prompt templates, constrained decoding) would produce fewer invalid first‑pass candidates.

Why the guarded path was not exercised. The guarded pipeline had no effect because deterministic_netops_validator_v5 reported valid = true for every shared_initial_candidate in the confirmatory sample. The validator's decision relied on matching parsed_command_count to required_command_count and satisfying workflow_policies encoded in each task_manifest entry (for example, "must_be_down_for_fields", "final_group_constraints"). Where those constraints were present the shared candidates adhered to the required_sequence in all 200 pairs. The archived validator_trace subtables provide per‑episode evidence: validation_before.normalized_configuration equals validation_after.normalized_configuration and violation_count = 0 for each episode, so repair_applied remained false across the run.

Threats to validity (artifact‑grounded). Internal validity: the paired design with shared_initial_candidate correctly isolates validator/repair effects but prevents measurement of generation variability. Construct validity: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 enforces syntactic and workflow‑policy checks; it is a static validator that does not execute vendor CLI on physical devices nor perform packet‑level emulation. Thus, validator.valid is an abstraction that does not capture runtime behavior (timing, protocol interactions, emergent forwarding anomalies). External validity: the experiment used one declared generator (gpt‑5‑mini via openai_responses), one deterministic synthetic task bank, and one validator implementation; generalization beyond these artifacts is unsupported by the archived evidence. Conclusion validity: zero discordant outcomes preclude estimation of repair effectiveness magnitude under different sampling regimes because the guarded path was never invoked.

Concrete preregistered follow‑on estimand variants. The archived artifacts and preregistration explicitly recorded several alternative estimands and design changes that would allow the repair path to be exercised: (A) remove shared_initial_candidate semantics so baseline and guarded arms receive independent first‑pass samples (this requires revising the paired analysis to account for sampling variability but exercises repair on a wider set of faulty generators outputs); (B) select or synthesize tasks labeled "extreme" difficulty or inject adversarial perturbations into generated candidates to raise the expected validator failure rate; (C) set explicit non‑null temperature values and preregister temperature sweeps to study diversity‑vs‑failure tradeoffs; (D) increase validator fidelity by integrating vendor CLI semantics and packet‑level emulation for runtime verification; (E) expand to multi‑model sampling to assess generality across generator families. Each follow‑on variant is grounded in the execution and task manifest artifacts archived with this run and can be implemented without inventing new infrastructure beyond the documented adapter and validator interfaces.

Operational implications and safe deployment notes. The null effect observed here is a narrowly scoped artifact: it shows that, for this synthetic task bank and this particular sampling semantics, every sampled candidate already satisfied the deterministic validator and so no repairs were required. It does not imply that GVR pipelines are unnecessary in practice. In production settings, task diversity, adversarial inputs, or model‑sampling settings that increase first‑pass error rates would be expected to produce validator detections and thus exercise repairs. Operational validation should therefore (a) include independent sampling of generations, (b) exercise adversarial/edge cases representative of operational risk, and (c) integrate runtime emulation or staged rollouts to capture dynamic interactions not represented in static validators.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory experiment measuring the downstream effect of a deterministic validator plus one permitted automated repair on the exact same sampled LLM candidate per intent (shared_initial_candidate semantics). Using gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 on 200 paired intents, every shared initial candidate passed validation; no repairs were attempted or applied; baseline and guarded outcomes were identical (paired difference = 0.0; McNemar p = 1.0; paired bootstrap CI = [0.0, 0.0]). This artifact‑grounded null result demonstrates an estimand boundary: under shared_initial_candidate semantics and the executed task bank the guarded pipeline had no opportunity to alter outcomes. To evaluate repair efficacy under realistic sampling variability and adversarial conditions, preregistered follow‑on experiments that remove shared_initial_candidate semantics, increase task difficulty or adversariality, set explicit sampling parameters, and raise validator fidelity are required. The full execution and analysis artifacts archived with this run permit exact reproduction of the executed estimand and provide a stable base for precisely defined extensions.

limitations: Shared_initial_candidate semantics: the design produced exactly one sampled initial generation per intent and reused it across baseline and guarded conditions; this measures validator/repair effects only and cannot detect differences caused by independent per‑condition sampling or prompt engineering.

Temperature unset (temperature = null) in the archived model configuration: null/unset is not evidence of deterministic sampling and does not imply temperature = 0; sampling nondeterminism may still have occurred during the single sampled generation.
Single model and single hosted provider: results reflect gpt‑5‑mini under the archived adapter; generalization to other models or model families is unsupported by these artifacts.

Synthetic task bank and validator abstraction: tasks were synthetic 'intent_configuration_repair_v1' items and the deterministic validator is a static abstraction; realistic vendor CLI idiosyncrasies, emergent runtime interactions, and hardware effects were not executed on live devices.

No observed validator failures: all initial candidates were validator‑valid, so the experiment could not assess the repair step's effectiveness; the null effect therefore reflects the task bank and sampling semantics rather than evidence that GVR pipelines are unnecessary in general.
